content:
Transferring keyboard shortcuts to a programmable macro keyboard is one of the best productivity tricks I've ever done.

A keyboard shortcut exploration journey

My initial foray into keyboard shortcuts was using simple macOS text replacements, such as @@ for my primary email address, with full name, address, phone number, zip code, etc. handled the same way.

From there, I decided to take things to another level with Keyboard Maestro, starting with shortcuts to open several frequently used folders and applications.

From desktop to downloads to work-related folders, Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, taking me places instantly that would otherwise require several mouse clicks. Other function keys are used to launch frequently used applications and websites, as well as to access Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

This later evolved into automating parts of my workflow, including launching QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically opening Shure PlusMOTIV when I plug in a specific USB-C microphone.

Soon, I was also customizing shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panel configurations, some of which I quickly moved to the Logitech MX Master for faster editing.

Taking it up a notch

I used this setup for quite a long time, until one day Gui Rambo from 9to5Mac told me about a small macro keyboard he bought with 12 keys and 3 knobs. I was immediately intrigued and bought one just like it.

When it arrived, I first realized that getting it set up to work properly on macOS required some extra effort. Fortunately, a GitHub project had already done most of the work, and with ChatGPT's help, I got it sorted out smoothly.

One benefit of this setup is that with a dedicated keyboard to trigger Keyboard Maestro shortcuts, I don't have to deliberately memorize them, nor do I have to make ergonomic compromises.

Moreover, since this keyboard can be configured with up to 3 layers of 12 macro keys each, plus knobs (which themselves can also function as buttons), I can have one way of operating when working in Adobe Audition, and a completely different way when interacting with the system.

When using Adobe Audition, combining this macro keyboard with the MX Master, switching tools, exporting files (or just exporting specific sections), applying effects like normalization, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, ripple delete, etc.—the speed and smoothness is on a completely different level compared to using regular keyboard shortcuts, or worse, no shortcuts at all.

When going back to using the system, I can switch the same keyboard to another layer to switch audio input, adjust volume, adjust screen brightness, mute or unmute the microphone, and just as easily access frequently used folders.

Admittedly, memorizing all these commands did take me some time, but they become reflexive much faster than you'd think. More importantly, when I have to work without it, honestly, it feels like my Mac is broken.

Beyond that, there are countless macro keyboard configurations and options on the market, with different shapes, sizes, key counts, knobs, and lighting colors. This exploration path really seems endless, and if your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn't?), I sincerely recommend you check it out.
